text: The final lesson of this course — a real code review of the equipment-checkout application built over the last three lessons, then a look at what's next.

First, performance. The availability check already used hasNext rather than getRowCount, but it's worth stating why that matters. getRowCount forces the database to count every matching row before your code even looks at one. hasNext only needs to find one. For a request table that might eventually hold years of history, that's the difference between a query that scales and one that silently gets slower every year.

Next, the Business Rule itself. A review checks three things — when it runs, which table and operation it's scoped to, and whether its condition matches the intent. It's before insert, scoped to the request table, insert only. Adding an explicit condition checking that equipment isn't empty documents that intent for the next developer, and skips the query entirely on the rare empty case.

Stepping back, this four-lesson build is a working application. A scoped application boundary from Chapter 5. A real data model with a reference field from Chapter 6. A class-based Script Include from Chapter 3. A before-insert Business Rule from Chapter 1. A GlideAjax-backed Client Script from Chapter 2, confirmed to stay properly isolated. Every chapter in this course contributed one real piece to one real, running application.

But it's not finished in an absolute sense. There's no REST-accessible endpoint for an external system to create a request, and no outbound integration to notify anything when equipment goes overdue. Those gaps aren't oversights — they're deliberately out of scope here, the same way Lesson 31 flagged them.

This course is complete. The next course in this path, ServiceNow IntegrationHub and REST APIs, picks up exactly where this one left off — authentication schemes, outbound calls, and the integration patterns this capstone's application still needs.
